paragraphs: The fires in Chang’an began in the West Market.

At first there was only a thread of smoke behind a fodder merchant’s rear wall. The traders were closing shop, carrying hemp sacks indoors, when several cracks sounded overhead and the dry grass caught. Flame raced along the roofline, illuminating the last mourning banners for Wang Meng still clinging to the ward wall. People from half the street came running with buckets. A Di carter tore open the shop doors; a Xianbei apprentice went into the flames to drag out fodder. None had time to distinguish another man’s accent.

The proprietor was named Hexi. As a young man he had crossed the river with a Yan army and injured his left leg; he now walked with a severe limp. Leaning on a staff, he tried to rush into the flames, crying that his account books were still under the counter. A Di carter seized him around the waist. “If the books burn, write them again! If you burn, where are we supposed to find another you?”

Before he finished, there was a dull report in the courtyard. An earthenware jar burst in the heat, driving hot oil and broken tiles through the doorway and knocking down two rescuers. The carter’s sleeve caught at once. Hexi knelt and beat at it with his staff, singeing half his own beard.
Then someone at the end of the street shouted, “Yan men have set fire to a Di carriage yard!”
From the other direction came the answer: “Di soldiers are robbing Yan shops under cover of the fire!”

Buckets stopped in midair. Men edged toward familiar faces. Axes brought to break down walls and poles used for carrying loads became weapons in a heartbeat. The fire was already climbing toward the adjoining hay store, yet someone swung at a man across the road. When the patrol entered the street, those lying on the ground were no longer only victims of the flames.
At that very hour, a new imperial decree appeared in Yanshou Ward in the north of the city.

It had government paper, a vermilion seal, and the script customarily used by the central drafting office. Nothing was missing. From this month onward, it declared, Qiang and Xianbei military households were to be relocated. Their men would serve with the army beyond the frontier; their families would be registered where they remained. Any refusal would be treated as defiance of an imperial decree. The ward elder read it a third time and still could not believe his eyes. He wiped them with his sleeve. Another old man, who could read, came to examine the seal and ran a finger over it for a long while. He kept saying it looked genuine.

Soon wheels creaked and locks clattered throughout the ward. Parents roused children from their beds; others took down old bows unused for years and blew off the dust. A Qiang woman stood in her courtyard with a child in her arms and asked her husband who would own the newly planted vegetable patch behind their house if he left that day. He took a long time to answer, and in the end only pushed another grain sack deeper into the cart.

The rumor traveled faster than the carts. Between Yanshou and Yongning, “military households are to be moved” became “wives and daughters will be left in the capital,” and then “all the men’s horses will be confiscated.” One speaker claimed to have seen an even longer secret order on the ward gate. Somehow he could not say on which wall it had been hung.

The family of a Xianbei officer in Yongning tried to leave the city by night and was turned back by a patrol. In the shouting, a blade opened a gate guard’s shoulder, and the ward gates were barred. Someone within saw the mass of torches outside and imagined government soldiers preparing to slaughter everyone in the ward. He set an empty house ablaze, sending a second fire above the city walls. When the capital prefecture rang its bell, several street gates closed at once, convincing still more people that something momentous was happening. Someone had written on a wall: “Yan men will kill the Di tonight.” Two alleys away appeared: “Di troops will massacre the ward at dawn.” Those who read both lines corroborated one another; not one had seen who held the brush.

Fu Jian received the reports while examining the evidence left by Sun Fu and the horse dealer with Fu Rong. The fine black thread, wrapped in white paper, lay at the edge of the desk, awaiting examination by the textile experts. An attendant brought in the forged decree, its edge stained with wall dust. Quan Yi needed only a glance at the vermilion seal to see that one stroke sat a fraction out of place. Fu Rong did not immediately order a citywide proclamation denouncing the forgery.
“Why should the people believe this sheet?” he asked.
“Because the seal looks genuine,” Quan Yi said with a frown.
“Also because it says aloud what they have been thinking about at night and have been afraid to ask.”

Fu Jian spread the decree flat. Side by side, the forged order was startlingly plain: relocate, confiscate, punish disobedience. The genuine military reform edict spoke of validating service rolls, rotating units, settling families, and assessing cavalry horses. Even ministers needed the regulations beside them to make sense of its elaborations. He remembered Wang Meng’s hand in Chengming Hall, cold as paper soaked by rain. Wang Meng had lived long enough to tell him to take armies out of the hands of their former masters. He had not lived long enough to decide where the thirty thousand soldiers' wives and children would reside, or which tally a man should show when leading his horse outside the gate.

“Keep the troops in their camps,” Fu Jian ordered. “No formed units entering wards where military families live. Send fire crews to fight fires and separate patrols to arrest arsonists. Wherever a decree is suspect, preserve the paper and examine its seal. Do not beat the person who posted it to death on the spot.”
The capital prefect was sweating. “Several wards refuse to open their gates. If the Guards do not enter, Majesty, I fear we cannot quiet them.”
“Then I’ll go.”

Fu Hong followed his father out of the palace. That afternoon he had been checking the fallen soldier’s name with the clerks of the First Battalion; tonight he saw his father dressing in haste, the gray at his temples painfully clear in lamplight. He almost spoke a word of protest, but let it pass. At the carriage, he merely asked whether they should take the authentic decree from the Secretariat.
“Take it,” Fu Jian said. “And some blank wooden tallies.”
“What are those for?”
“If people ask where they are to be sent, we cannot simply tell them to go home and wait for the government.”

Half the gate at Yanshou Ward had been broken. Carts filled the lane one behind another. Servant women carried infants, boys guarded cart shafts, and men with bows bound to their arms could not bring themselves to lift a hand from their children’s shoulders. When Fu Jian’s carriage arrived, a rustle ran through the street. Someone even asked, in a low voice, whether the Heavenly King’s own banner was real.
Fu Jian got down and walked toward them with only Fu Hong, the capital prefect, and a dozen guards. The old Qiang ward elder, gray in hair and beard, was pushed forward holding a torn-down notice.
“Can you read?” Fu Jian asked.
“A little.”
“Then you couldn’t see what was wrong?”
“I can recognize an official seal,” the old man replied. “And what the paper orders has happened to us before.”

Fu Jian stopped. The elder said he had lived in Longxi when young and been moved twice by passing armies. Once they called it protection from disorder, once resettlement for food. Each time they had promised land; each time the family had spent three winters beside a ditch before they received any. His grandson had only just learned to write his own name on the wall. If they had to leave again, he feared the boy would never find even that wall.
When he finished, Fu Jian ordered the capital prefect to read out the true military edict in the street. Yet the words “rotation” and “resettlement” only raised more questions.
“If my husband is rotated away, where do I live with the children?” one woman asked.
“Whose are the horses that belonged to the old regiment?”
“Is the land being issued by officials, or does it already belong to someone?”
“What if they promise grain, then refuse it halfway along the road?”

The prefect’s answers came more and more slowly. He tried to find the relevant provisions, only to discover that not one was detailed enough for the people standing beside these carts to follow when they set out that day.

Fu Hong took the blank wooden tallies from an attendant and gave them to the elder. “No household is to be driven out tonight. Tomorrow, bring three respected people from the ward to the Secretariat. Record each family’s names, residence, horses, and land deeds, one by one. Write disputed matters on the reverse, and leave a copy here. Until a destination and grain allotment are known, no army clerk may order these carts to move.”
A woman suddenly asked, “Once you’ve written it down, who will acknowledge it?”
“The Secretariat and capital prefecture must check it together. If the army wants to move a family, it must sign the same register.”
The woman said nothing. The elder asked, “And if none of those three offices will take responsibility?”

Fu Hong opened his mouth. He thought of the soldiers examining passes at the camp gate earlier that day and paused. “Keep hold of the tally first. Once it exists, there must be somewhere you can bring it for an answer.”
Fu Jian looked at his son, then ordered the prefect to add his own name. “If anyone refuses to register them tomorrow, send me his name.”

Gradually people began unloading bedding and carrying it back indoors. Some would not set down their knives. The elder asked whether the ward gate could remain unbarred that night, rather than imprison entire families inside. A patrol captain protested that the night curfew must be enforced. Fu Jian told him to stand aside. Patrolmen and military households would each appoint guards at the gate, sign their names, and reconsider matters at dawn.
“Tonight, keep this street safe,” Fu Jian told the elder. “Tomorrow I shall have the next steps written here for you to read.”

The elder bowed without thanking him and went back to persuade those still determined to flee. At the ward entrance, Fu Jian listened to cart shafts being lowered, one after another: the soft thuds of hearts long suspended in fear settling back into their owners' chests.

Outside Yanshou, more than a dozen bodies lay beside the road. A small pair of feet protruded from beneath one straw mat; one wore a newly sewn cloth shoe. The prefect said casualties in the West Market and Yongning were still being counted, among them children crushed in the stampedes whose names were not yet known. Fu Jian stepped forward and bent to cover the feet with the mat.

By the time they reached the West Market, the fodder shop had burned hollow. Embers glowed faintly under wet roof tiles. Hexi sat by the broken wall holding a few scorched pages from his ledgers. The Di carter who had helped save him leaned against the wall with his burned arm bandaged, breathing heavily. Both had been injured, yet they sat apart and neither raised his eyes. Fu Jian asked nothing about who had struck first. He ordered the patrol to clear fallen roof timbers so water carts could pass. As he went by, Hexi muttered a curse. Fu Jian could not hear every word but understood that it was aimed at his government. He walked on.

The council after dawn was unusually long. Smoke from the night before still clung to the ministers' sleeves, yet their opinions were remarkably alike: stop for now. The imperial kinsmen feared forcing the old military factions into open revolt; Xianbei and Qiang ministers feared that the next true decree might become indistinguishable from the forgery; Han officials feared the absence of funds and grain. Yao Chang rose to propose suspending mixed recruitment across the provinces for half a year, leaving only the First Battalion as a trial, and resuming the work after both the Ye and Chang’an cases had been solved. He had spent the previous day guarding the palace. His court clothes were immaculate; his face was worn with fatigue. Nothing in his proposal was easily faulted.

Fu Jian heard him out and looked over the officials below the steps. A six-month pause might mean one less fire tonight. He did not despise the suggestion. Since leaving the West Market, he seemed unable to lose the smell of charred wood and ointment.
“Father,” Fu Hong said, stepping forward, “I ask that we handle this in three parts.”

The hall grew quiet. Fu Hong did not raise his voice; he had an assistant unfold three memoranda already written. The first proposed three months to verify dispatches and grain vouchers around the capital. Service registers and ration books must be surrendered for inspection; no former commander could keep a private roll. The second proposed keeping the First Battalion in training for six months while spreading the amalgamation of provincial forces over three years. Men, rations, and service credit were to be checked before any garrison was moved. The third required land, grain, destinations, and arrangements for accompanying families to be verified before any military household was relocated. Government cavalry horses and privately owned property were to have separate registers; officials could not seal a ward or seize land by invoking the residents' ancestry.
Fu Mo asked, “What if the old contingents refuse rotation during those three years?”

“Submission of rolls and ration vouchers cannot wait three years,” Fu Hong replied. “If they refuse, suspend their pay for verification. If they raise private troops against the order, investigate that as an offense. Keeping a trial battalion does not authorize anyone to recruit an army of his own.”

Pei Xuan warned that merging the records would overburden provincial clerks. Fu Hong acknowledged the need for more clerks, more accounts, and the certainty of mistakes. Wrong entries must be open to review. But the excuse that there was too much paperwork could not justify returning the recovered army tallies to the old generals.
Listening nearby, Yao Chang smiled suddenly. “Your Highness’s three measures all require men to carry them out. Does Chang’an have so many capable people?”
“Not at present,” Fu Hong replied. “If we do nothing for that reason, we shall have none next year either.”

Fu Jian remained silent a long while. At last he looked toward Yao Chang. “Your wish to slow matters is well meant. Had we sent three thousand more men into the wards last night, still more might be dead.”
Yao Chang lowered his head. Fu Jian continued: “We may go more slowly. But we cannot let those who set the fires dictate the government’s pace.”

The new edict was not finished in the hall. For three days, the Secretariat, army administration, and capital prefecture argued over who must advance grain when counties ran short, which old register would furnish the pensions of soldiers killed in earlier campaigns, and where resettled families might complain if they disputed their allotments. Fu Hong spread the wooden tallies collected in Yanshou across the floor and made the clerks fill in destinations that could be verified. Quan Yi complained that he was taking too long. Fu Hong asked him to look at one child’s name: the boy’s father served in Beidi, his grandmother lived beyond Ba Bridge. If the resettlement map erred by half a road, the three might never meet again.

The revised decree, when posted, was several times longer than the forgery. Old people came to read it and frowned before they had finished half a page. Young people crowded close to make out the characters; some still distrusted it when they reached the end. The Secretariat set a second, plainer board beside it. In large characters it stated three points: no households moved this month; a deadline for surrendering military registers; no relocation without verified land and grain. Even those unable to read official prose could have the meaning explained. Beside the forgery, the new notice still traveled less quickly than rumor. At least some people now stopped to ask questions.

The verified findings from the First Battalion murder were also read aloud outside the south gate. Sun Fu was dead; the horse dealer had died in a prison guarded by soldiers; the investigators could not assemble the whole conspiracy into a tidy confession. The army surgeon reported only the wounds he had examined. Officials displayed the wooden tokens, hemp rope, and gold. Fu Rong explained item by item what was proven and what remained conjecture. Many remained unconvinced. Someone shouted, “If you couldn’t even keep those two alive, why should we trust your investigation?”
“Our inquiry fell short. That is the government’s fault,” Fu Rong said. “Where the testimony is missing, it remains missing. Anyone who knows more should report to the Court of Justice.”
A low, derisive laugh passed through the crowd. He did not forbid it.

When Helai Yan’s wife and daughter arrived from Chang’an, his coffin stood in a thin-roofed shelter. The little girl clutched a length of red thread she had meant to tie to her father’s knife. Liang Hu was summoned as a witness. She looked up at him. “Were you and my father good friends?”

Liang Hu froze. Zhao An began to speak for him, then stopped. Liang Hu remembered the dung baskets in the stable, the wooden bar that divided their sleeping places, and the knife Helai Yan had given back to him freshly sharpened.
“Not very good,” he said. “We argued a lot.”
Some of the light went out of the child’s eyes.
“But he sharpened my knife. I carried his arrows.” Liang Hu looked at the coffin. “If he’d lived, perhaps one day we’d have got along.”

The girl bowed her head and tied the red thread around a wooden catch on the coffin. Her mother was no longer young. She did not wail; she merely asked that her husband’s military death allowance and compensation as a murder victim be entered separately on the army rolls, so the family would not have to travel between two offices later. Fu Hong heard and handed the wooden tally bearing Helai Yan’s name to the clerk responsible for service pensions. He made the clerk write down, in her presence, where she was to claim the money.

A Qin banner covered the coffin at burial. Some thought Helai Yan’s wife would object, but she smoothed the corner of the cloth and said, “It was Qin rations he drew at the end.” She offered no explanation. The mountains and rivers of Yan lay far away; her family’s rice jar was still in Chang’an.

Liang Hu, Zhao An, Manu, and Zhai Hei carried the coffin out of the city. Their steps did not match. On the first stretch they nearly knocked the bier off its poles. They glanced at one another and gradually found a common pace. Days later, a young Qiang soldier was sent to fill the gap in their squad. He knew nobody, understood none of Liang Hu’s orders, and stood timidly at the tent door with an old bow, staring at the wooden bar dividing their beds. Manu brought him inside and translated the first rule: no stealing another man’s sleeping place at night.

In Chang’an, house frames were going up again. The broken half of the Yanshou gate stood propped against a wall, with patrolmen and military families taking turns on watch. Hexi spread the blackened pages of his accounts to dry, one by one. The Di carter with the injured arm passed by and dropped two bundles of usable horse fodder beside him, walking on before Hexi could speak. Hexi chased him half a step on his staff, then called across the street, “I’ll put it on your account!”

At dusk, Fu Jian passed the Secretariat and saw an old man questioning a clerk beneath the new decree. If the land promised to a relocated military household never materialized, whom should they appeal to? The clerk answered: the Secretariat. And if the Secretariat ignored them? The Court of Justice. Fu Jian stood below the steps listening. The old man turned, saw him, and said without fear, “Heavenly King, men grow old.”

Fu Jian looked through the doorway into the lamplight. Fu Hong and several clerks were arguing fiercely; someone had copied two mu incorrectly in a land register and was striking the desk. The voices rose and fell behind the lattice window, nothing like the polished memorials read in court.
“Yes,” Fu Jian told the old man. “Which is why their names must go into the registers, for those who come after us to examine.”
The old man did not seem satisfied. He bowed nevertheless and went slowly away.

A wind came from the West Market, still bearing a trace of burned timber. Outside the gate the two decrees hung side by side. A corner of the forgery was already curled and torn; the genuine one was on thicker paper, nailed firmly in place, with the evening light falling across the newly added characters for “land and grain.” Children chased one another in the alley, kicking dust onto the paper. The words remained legible.
